authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring assistant

items.prompt: A candidate proposes binary search over indices of an unsorted array to find a target value. No predicate over index is monotonic. What is the decisive evaluation?
constraints: The array is unsorted.
No monotonic predicate over indices is given.
The candidate claims binary search on index.

options.text: Accept it because inspecting a midpoint always reduces the remaining index interval.
Accept it because target equality is a Boolean predicate.
Reject it: a midpoint comparison cannot prove that either half contains no valid answer.

feedback.reason: Binary search is legal only when each observation justifies discarding a contiguous part of the search domain. An arbitrary unsorted index domain provides no such implication.

blocks.text: Shrinking an interval is not sufficient; the discarded interval must be proven irrelevant. In sorted exact search, comparison with the midpoint establishes which side can still contain the target. In answer-space search, a monotonic feasibility predicate establishes a boundary. In the unsorted array [1, 100, 2], searching for 2 and comparing with midpoint value 100 cannot justify discarding the right half: doing so would discard the answer itself. Equal and unequal values can appear anywhere, so a midpoint observation says nothing about either side. The transfer rule is to state the legal half-discard implication explicitly before accepting any logarithmic search.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_log: Mechanically moving a boundary can make the loop short while making the result wrong. This option becomes valid only when an ordering or monotonic predicate proves the discarded half impossible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_numeric: Every equality test is Boolean, but Boolean output is not the same as monotonicity over the search domain. It becomes useful for binary search only when false and true values form an ordered boundary.

items.prompt: A candidate uses a variable sliding window for the shortest subarray with sum at least T: expand when the sum is too small and shrink when it is large enough. Values may be negative. Is the strategy legal?
constraints: The answer must be contiguous.
Values may be negative.
The proposed rule moves each boundary only forward.

options.text: Reject it: adding or removing a value can move the sum in either direction, so the local repair rule can skip the optimum.
Accept it because each boundary advances at most n times, which gives linear work and therefore guarantees the optimal window is retained.
Accept it because the desired answer is contiguous, so two forward-moving boundaries are sufficient to represent every relevant candidate.

feedback.reason: Contiguity does not guarantee a monotone validity repair rule. Negative values break the movement implication used by the proposed window.

blocks.text: The standard variable-window argument needs more than two boundaries: boundary motion must change validity predictably. With nonnegative values, expanding cannot reduce the sum and shrinking cannot increase it. Negative values remove both guarantees. For a concrete failure, use a = [1, -1, 5] and T = 5:

items: After reading 1 and then -1, the running sums are 1 and 0, both below T, so the rule never advances the left boundary.
After reading 5, the window [1, -1, 5] has sum 5, so the algorithm records length 3.
It removes the leftmost 1, obtains sum 4, and stops shrinking because the sum is below T.
The optimal window [5] has length 1, but reaching it requires removing -1 even though that increases the sum; the proposed repair rule never does so.

blocks.text: Linear pointer movement proves only the running time of the implemented process, not its correctness. The transfer rule is to reject a window whenever validity is not repairable by one-direction boundary moves under the stated value domain.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_contiguous: Contiguity makes a window representation possible, but not sufficient. The option becomes valid only when the aggregate and constraints also support a monotone repair rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_linear: An O(n) execution can still return the wrong answer. The movement count becomes relevant only after the invariant proves that every discarded window is safely excluded.

items.prompt: To find whether any two values sum to T, a candidate places pointers at the two ends of the original unsorted array and moves left or right according to whether the current sum is below or above T. What should happen?
constraints: The original array is unsorted.
The candidate uses sum comparison to move endpoints.
No preprocessing is included.

options.text: Accept it because opposite-end pointers cover the whole array and every move reduces the number of unexamined endpoint pairs.
Accept it when all values are distinct, because removing duplicate ambiguity makes the sum comparison determine a safe movement direction.
Reject it: without an ordering relation, moving either pointer does not safely eliminate all pairs involving that endpoint.

feedback.reason: The sum comparison guides pointer movement only when the remaining values are ordered. Original endpoints in an unsorted array carry no discard implication.

blocks.text: In a sorted array, a sum below T proves that the current smallest value cannot pair with any remaining value to reach T, so advancing the left pointer is safe. A sum above T similarly justifies decreasing the right pointer. The original order provides no such implication. For a = [4, 1, 6, 2] and T = 10, the endpoint sum 4 + 2 = 6 is too small, so the proposed rule advances the left pointer and permanently discards 4; it thereby loses the only solution, 4 + 6. Distinctness removes duplicate values but does not create order. The transfer rule is to identify the comparison-to-discard implication behind every pointer move; pointer count and geometry alone do not establish legality.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_two_ends: Opposite ends are a representation, not a proof. They become a legal movement scheme only when ordering or another invariant makes an endpoint provably dominated.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_if_unique: Unique values avoid duplicate handling but do not tell which direction changes the sum. The claim becomes valid only after a suitable ordering or monotone relation is established.

items.prompt: A candidate builds prefix minima P[i] = min(a[0..i]) and claims that, for l > 0, the minimum of any inclusive range [l, r] can be recovered by 'subtracting' P[l-1] from P[r], analogous to prefix sums. Is the mechanism legal?
constraints: The array is static.
The query asks for arbitrary range minima.
The candidate stores only one prefix minimum per position.

options.text: Accept it because the array never changes, so every prefix minimum remains valid and can be reused for any later range query.
Accept it because every prefix aggregate supports constant-time range queries.
Reject it: minimum has no inverse operation that removes the contribution of the earlier prefix.

feedback.reason: Prefix range recovery requires an aggregate that can remove the earlier prefix contribution. Minimum is not invertible by subtraction or an equivalent cancellation rule.

blocks.text: Prefix sums work because sum([l, r]) = prefix[r] − prefix[l − 1]; subtraction cancels the earlier values. Minimum has no corresponding inverse. For a = [1, 5, 4], the prefix minima are P = [1, 1, 1]. Query [1, 2] has minimum 4, but P[2] = 1 is controlled by the excluded a[0], and P[0] = 1 does not reveal whether 4, 5, or any other value remains. Subtraction even produces 0, which is not the answer. Static input makes preprocessing stable but cannot restore discarded information. The transfer rule is to reject a prefix-derived range query unless the stored aggregate and recovery operation preserve enough information to isolate the requested range.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_prefix_name: The word prefix describes where data was aggregated, not whether arbitrary subranges are recoverable. The claim is valid for aggregates with a suitable inverse or richer structure, not for every operation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_static: Static data prevents stale preprocessing, but the representation can still be insufficient. Static range minimum needs a different structure or additional information.

items.prompt: A candidate inserts all distinct values into an ordinary hash set whose contract does not guarantee iteration order, then returns that iteration order as the required ascending list. What is the correct legality decision?
constraints: Output values must be distinct.
Output values must be ascending.
The candidate performs no sorting step.

options.text: Accept it because expected O(1) insertion implies ordered output.
Reject it: membership uniqueness does not provide the required ascending-order invariant.
Accept it because removing duplicates is the only hard part.

feedback.reason: A hash set can establish uniqueness, but it does not establish ascending order. The candidate fails the output contract unless it adds an ordering step.

blocks.text: Strategies must preserve every required output property, not merely compute a related set. Hashing is a good mechanism for presence and uniqueness, but ordinary hash iteration has no sorted-order guarantee. A legal composite candidate could deduplicate with a set and then sort the distinct values, but that has a different cost model. Expected insertion time says nothing about iteration order. The transfer rule is to reject any candidate whose maintained state omits a required ordering, ranking, witness, or multiplicity property.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_unique: Uniqueness is necessary but incomplete because the output explicitly requires ascending order. This becomes valid only when the contract permits arbitrary order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_expected: Expected lookup complexity is unrelated to ordering semantics. The statement would require an ordered set or a separate sorting mechanism, not a faster hash operation.

items.prompt: For every index, a task must output all greater values to its right. A candidate claims an O(n) monotonic stack can pop dominated values permanently and still enumerate every required pair. What is the decisive response?
constraints: Every greater pair must be emitted.
The candidate pops values permanently.
Output size may be quadratic.

options.text: Reject it: popped values can remain required for other outputs, and the result itself can contain Θ(n²) pairs.
Accept it because the comparison asks for greater values to the right, which is the defining signal for a decreasing monotonic stack.
Accept it because each value is pushed and popped at most once, so all required greater relationships can be reported within linear work.

feedback.reason: The standard pop-once invariant supports nearest or next-greater queries, not enumeration of all greater pairs. The output size alone can exceed linear time.

blocks.text: A monotonic stack discards candidates that are dominated for a specific future query, such as the nearest greater element. When every greater relation must be output, a value popped for one comparison may still participate in many later result pairs, so permanent discard loses required information. For a strictly increasing array, the number of reported pairs is n(n-1)/2, establishing an output-sensitive lower bound. The push/pop amortization proves the internal stack work only for a legal invariant; it cannot erase required output. The transfer rule is to match a dominance discard rule to the exact answer contract and account for output size.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_each_once: Push/pop accounting proves linear stack operations, but not that the stack retains all required relationships. It becomes valid for contracts such as nearest greater where dominated candidates are truly irrelevant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_greater: A surface keyword is insufficient. Monotonic stacks require a specific nearest/dominance boundary; they are not universal for every comparison involving greater values.

items.prompt: Select all candidates that must be rejected under the stated contracts.
constraints: Evaluate legality, not relative performance.
Select all candidates whose stated preconditions are insufficient.
Do not infer unstated sorting, positivity, or mutation constraints.

options.text: Binary search for a value in an unsorted array with no monotonic predicate.
Opposite-end two pointers for pair sum after values are sorted.
A sum-based variable window that shrinks when too large even though values may be negative.
Prefix sums for many static range-sum queries.

feedback.reason: The binary-search and window candidates lack their required discard or movement invariants. The sorted two-pointer and static prefix-sum candidates have the stated preconditions needed for legality.

blocks.text: A legality audit checks each candidate's proof obligation before ranking efficiency:

items: Reject unsorted binary search: a midpoint observation supplies no implication that makes either contiguous half impossible.
Keep sorted two pointers: value order makes a too-small sum safely eliminate the current minimum endpoint and a too-large sum eliminate the maximum endpoint.
Reject the negative-value window: adding or removing an element can reverse the sum direction, so its local shrink/expand rule can skip the optimum.
Keep static prefix sums: with P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i], subtraction P[r + 1] − P[l] cancels everything outside inclusive range [l, r], and static input keeps preprocessing current.

blocks.text: The transferable test is to name the invariant that licenses every discard, movement, or recovery operation. Apply that same gate to unfamiliar mechanisms before comparing their advertised performance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_two_pointer: This candidate is legal because sorting makes the sum comparison informative: a too-small sum safely eliminates the current minimum endpoint. It could still lose on mutation or cost, but those are later concerns.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.static_prefix_sum: This candidate is legal because sums are cancellable and the array does not change after preprocessing. It may be unnecessary for one query, but inefficiency or overengineering is not illegality.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.unsorted_binary: Omitting this rejection accepts interval halving without any proof that the discarded half lacks the target.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.negative_window: Omitting this rejection accepts a local movement rule whose sum can reverse direction when boundaries move.

items.prompt: A variable window advances left while invalid but never removes the outgoing element from its aggregate state. What is the legality decision?

options.text: Reject it until state and boundary movement are synchronized; the predicate is evaluated on the wrong range.
Accept it because left eventually reaches right and the loop terminates.
Accept it because each pointer moves at most n times.
Sorting automatically fixes the aggregate update without changing the implementation.

feedback.reason: A termination or runtime argument cannot legalize a state invariant that is already false.

blocks.text: When a boundary leaves, its contribution must leave the maintained state. Otherwise a later validity check refers to elements outside the candidate interval, so the algorithm can stop too late, score a wrong range, or miss a legal one. Fix the canonical update before comparing costs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_if_terminates: A terminating algorithm can still return an incorrect answer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_if_linear: Complexity does not prove state correctness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.replace_with_sort: Sorting does not update a range aggregate or preserve the original window contract.

items.prompt: A candidate uses ordinary BFS to minimize total cost in a graph whose edges have weights 1 and 7. What invariant failure justifies rejection?

options.text: BFS layers order edge count, not weighted path cost, so first discovery need not be cheapest.
BFS is illegal because weighted graphs cannot use visited state.
The queue must be replaced only because weighted graphs require a larger container.
BFS fails only when some edge weights are negative.

feedback.reason: The correctness invariant behind BFS is nondecreasing unit-distance layers, which does not match arbitrary nonnegative costs.

blocks.text: A path with two edges can cost 14 while a path with three edges costs 3. BFS may finalize the former first. A weighted method such as Dijkstra for nonnegative weights is needed; visited state remains useful under that method.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_forbidden: Weighted algorithms also track settled or relaxed vertices; the issue is ordering by cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_too_small: Container capacity is not the missing proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_edges_required: Different positive weights already break edge-count ordering.

items.prompt: A greedy candidate chooses the locally smallest next value, but no exchange argument or invariant connects that choice to a global optimum. What is the correct review result?

options.text: Reject or hold it as unproven until a safe-choice/exchange argument or counterexample analysis establishes correctness.
Accept it because a locally smallest choice is always compatible with a global minimum.
Accept it if its runtime is better than the reference, even without proof.
Ship it as exact because calling it a heuristic makes the proof unnecessary.

feedback.reason: Greedy correctness requires a theorem that makes the irreversible local choice safe; speed and naming cannot replace it.

blocks.text: A candidate may be experimentally useful or correct for a restricted domain, but an exact product contract needs a proof or an explicit counterexample boundary. The reference and constraints should remain available while the missing exchange argument is resolved.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_local_best: Local optimality does not imply global optimality without problem-specific structure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.accept_if_fast: A faster wrong algorithm is not a valid replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.label_heuristic_solution: Metadata cannot turn an unproven exact result into a correct implementation.

items.prompt: Why is ordinary BFS not a valid shortest-path strategy when edges have arbitrary positive weights?
constraints: The objective is minimum total edge weight.
Edge weights are not all equal.

options.text: FIFO order tracks edge count rather than accumulated weight, so Dijkstra or another weighted method is required.
options.explanation: The unweighted BFS invariant no longer matches the objective.

options.text: BFS remains correct because every edge is traversed once.
options.explanation: Traversal count does not equal path cost.

options.text: Sort edges once and then run ordinary BFS to make levels represent weight.
options.explanation: Edge order does not convert weighted paths into unit edges.

options.text: BFS fails only when weights are negative; arbitrary positive weights are safe.
options.explanation: Different positive weights already break depth-cost equivalence.

feedback.reason: A strategy is illegal when its traversal order proves the wrong objective.

blocks.text: BFS is correct for unit-cost edges because depth equals path cost. With weighted edges, a deeper path can be cheaper or a shallower path more expensive; Dijkstra's priority by distance restores the needed invariant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_weighted: Traversal count does not equal path cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_edges: Edge order does not convert weighted paths into unit edges.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_only: Different positive weights already break depth-cost equivalence.

items.prompt: What is the correct rejection reason for a greedy rule that has no feasible exchange or dominance proof?
constraints: The rule claims universal optimality.
The input domain includes legal adversarial cases.

options.text: Reject it as unproven until a safety property is established or a different strategy preserves alternatives.
options.explanation: Fast local choices are not correct by default.

options.text: Accept it if its asymptotic complexity is optimal, because correctness follows from speed.
Accept it after it passes representative examples.
options.explanation: Examples cannot quantify over all legal cases.

options.text: Mark it as a future-safe approach without changing the implementation.
options.explanation: A label does not supply a proof.

feedback.reason: The absence of a proof obligation is itself a strategy rejection signal.

blocks.text: A candidate may later be proved correct, but until the exchange, invariant, or state argument exists, it should not be presented as universally valid. The alternative may be DP, search, or a different greedy key.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.examples_enough: Examples cannot quantify over all legal cases.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.metadata: A label does not supply a proof.

items.prompt: Why should a positive-sum sliding-window strategy be rejected for arbitrary signed values when the target predicate is exact?
constraints: Negative values are legal.
The strategy shrinks while the sum is too large.

options.text: Adding or removing a value can move the sum in either direction, so the expand/shrink invariant is false; use prefix-based or another signed-safe state.
The strategy remains correct because a window is contiguous regardless of values.
options.explanation: Contiguity does not imply sum monotonicity.

options.text: Use a wider numeric type to restore the monotone movement proof.
options.explanation: Width fixes overflow, not sign behavior.

options.text: Sort values first so negatives appear before positives and the original subarray answers remain unchanged.
options.explanation: Sorting changes contiguity and index semantics.

feedback.reason: A strategy can be illegal because its core invariant is false under the new domain.

blocks.text: The issue is semantic, not numeric precision. Prefix sums plus a map can find exact signed ranges without assuming that pointer movements monotonically improve the sum.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_rule: Contiguity does not imply sum monotonicity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cast_numbers: Width fixes overflow, not sign behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_values: Sorting changes contiguity and index semantics.

items.prompt: Why should an in-place sort be rejected when the algorithm contract requires preserving input order and caller aliases?
constraints: Input mutation is forbidden.
Callers may retain references to the original collection.

options.text: In-place sorting changes observable input state; use a copy or a nonmutating approach and charge its resources.
options.explanation: A faster implementation is still illegal if it mutates forbidden state.

options.text: It is valid because sorting preserves the same values.
options.explanation: Order and aliases are part of the contract.

options.text: Copying is unnecessary because the sort result is all that callers need.
options.explanation: The stated caller contract requires the original unchanged.

options.text: Add a metadata flag saying mutation is acceptable without changing the API behavior.
options.explanation: Metadata cannot override the public contract.

feedback.reason: Strategy legality includes ownership, mutation, and aliasing constraints.

blocks.text: If sorting is otherwise the right algorithm, copy explicitly and report O(n) extra space/time. If that budget is disallowed, choose a strategy that works without mutating the input.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_same: Order and aliases are part of the contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.copy_free: The stated caller contract requires the original unchanged.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.flag_only: Metadata cannot override the public contract.
